title: Right Half Pyramid
description: Brute force to optimized: per-character printing versus building each row directly by its known length, then batching the whole pattern into one output call.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a positive integer n, print a right angled triangle of stars with n rows, where row i contains exactly i stars, left aligned.

blocks.text: Given a positive integer n, print a right angled triangle of stars with n rows, where row i contains exactly i stars, left aligned with no leading spaces.

blocks.title: Analogy: Stacking Growing Rows of Bricks
blocks.text: Picture stacking rows of bricks against a wall, where the very first row has just one brick, the next row has two, and each row after that has one more brick than the row above it. Every row starts flush against the same wall, so nothing ever needs to be shifted, each row is simply longer than the last.

blocks.caption: Row i always holds exactly i stars, growing from 1 up to n

blocks.content: {"headers":["Row","Output","Why"],"rows":[["Row 1","*","Row i always contains exactly i stars; row 1 has just one."],["Row 2","**","Row 2 has exactly two stars, one more than the row above it."],["Row 3","***","Row 3 continues the same one-more-star-per-row growth."],["Row 4","****","The final row, with exactly n stars."]]}

blocks.text: No rows at all, so nothing is printed.
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what is actually known ahead of time here.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Unlike a solid square, the rows here are not all identical, row i always has exactly i stars, one more than the row before it.

Observation 2: Even though the rows differ, the exact length of each row is completely known in advance, before that row is even started, since row i's length is simply the value i itself.

Observation 3: Whenever a row's exact length is known ahead of time, there is no need to grow it one character at a time, it can be built in a single direct operation instead, exactly the number of characters needed.

Observation 4: Since every row's construction is independent of the others, all n rows can be built first and then joined into one single string, letting the entire pattern be produced with just one output call.
That reasoning alone already reframes the problem: not "print each star" but "construct each already-known-length row directly."
Use an outer loop for each row i from 1 to n, and an inner loop that runs exactly i times, printing a single star character on every iteration.

items: Loop over each row i from 1 to n.
Inside that, loop exactly i times.
Print a single star for every one of those i iterations, one print call per character.
After finishing a row, move to the next line.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: print one star at a time, one call per character

codes.python:
def right_half_pyramid(n):
    for i in range(1, n + 1):                # row i needs exactly i stars
        for j in range(i):                    # print each of the i stars in this row
            print("*", end="")                  # one call per character
        print()                              # move to the next line after the row


if __name__ == "__main__":
    right_half_pyramid(4)

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The inner loop runs exactly i times for row i, deliberately tying the loop bound directly to the row number, since that relationship, row i needs i stars, is the entire definition of this shape.
A single star is printed per innermost iteration, the smallest possible unit of output, making the true per-character cost of this version fully visible.
The line break happens once per outer iteration, after the inner loop completes, since every row's stars must appear together before moving to the next line.

blocks.text: This is correct, since row i always ends up with exactly i stars printed, one at a time.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since the total number of stars across all rows is 1 plus 2 plus up to n, which is proportional to n squared, and each star costs its own print call.
Space: O(1) extra space, no string is ever built.

Limitation: printing one character at a time means as many output calls as there are stars, roughly n squared over 2 of them. Since the exact length of each row is already known in advance, that entire row can be built in a single operation instead, needing only one print call per row rather than one per character.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why printing one star at a time works but is wasteful: each row's exact length is already known the moment the outer loop reaches it, yet the brute force still grows it one character at a time.

What is being ignored: the fact that row i's length, i, is available immediately, with no need to discover it through repeated printing.

Can a row be built directly at its known length: yes, using a direct repeat operation that produces exactly i stars in one step.

What does that save: the number of print calls drops from roughly n squared over 2, the total star count, down to just n, one per row.

The core idea: for each row i, build a string of exactly i stars directly, then print it once.

For each row i, build a string of exactly i stars in one operation, using a direct repeat rather than appending characters one by one, then print that row with a single call. This cuts the number of print calls from roughly n squared down to just n, one per row.
For each row i, build the row directly at its known length using a repeat operation, then print it with a single call.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: build each row directly by its known length, one print call per row

blocks.text: This works because a row's length is determined entirely by its row number, known before that row is ever built, so directly repeating the star character exactly i times for row i produces precisely the same visible row as printing i individual stars would, just without needing to actually count up to i one print call at a time. Since every row's construction only depends on its own row number, nothing from any other row needs to be referenced or reused.

items: The row is built directly inside the outer loop, using i itself as the repeat count, so no separate length calculation or inner loop is needed at all.
A direct repeat operation constructs the entire row of i stars in one step, rather than appending one star at a time as the row number grows.
Each row is printed immediately after being built, one output call per row, rather than accumulating anything across rows at this stage.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) total characters produced, the same as the brute force, since that is the size of the output, but only O(n) print calls are made instead of O(n squared).
Space: O(n), for the single row string being built and printed at a time.
10. Further Optimization: A Single Output Call

Every row is already being built directly in one operation, so instead of printing each one separately, all n rows can be built first, joined together with newline characters, and the entire pattern can be produced with a single output call.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: join every row into one string and output it in a single call

items: Every row is still built directly at its own known length, i, exactly as in the optimized version, the only change is deferring output until every row exists.
Joining all n rows with newline characters assembles the complete multi-line pattern as a single string, entirely in memory, before any output call happens.
A single print call at the very end outputs the whole triangle, cutting the operation count down to exactly 1 regardless of how large n is.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the same total characters produced.
Space: O(n squared), to hold every row joined into one string before the single output call. This trades some memory for the fewest possible output calls, exactly one, no matter how large n is.

blocks.text: When a row length is already known ahead of time, there is no need to build it up one character at a time, it can be constructed directly in a single operation. And when the shape of every row is known in advance, all of the output work can be batched together, first at the row level and then, if useful, across the entire pattern at once.

items: Printing character by character even when the length of the row is already known before the inner loop starts.
Miscounting the number of stars per row, an off by one error here is one of the most common mistakes in pattern problems.
Forgetting the n = 0 edge case, where nothing at all should be printed.

blocks.text: This pattern is often the very first building block for more elaborate shapes, like pyramids with spaces or diamonds, so being fluent with exactly how row i relates to i stars is worth internalizing before moving on to shapes that mix stars and spaces together.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid growing the row one character at a time", think: build each row directly using its already-known length, i.
If the interviewer says "can you reduce this to one output call", think: build every row first, join them with newlines, print once.
If the interviewer says "why is this different from a solid square", think: here every row has a different, but still known in advance, length, rather than every row being identical.

Inverted pyramids and other patterns where each row's length is a simple, known function of the row number, reusing this same direct-construction idea.
Any output problem where the size of a piece of work is known before that work begins, favoring direct construction over incremental growth.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: All three versions produce the same O(n squared) total characters, since that is fixed by the shape itself. What changes is the number of output operations: roughly O(n squared) individual calls in the brute force version, O(n) calls in the optimized version, and exactly one call in the further optimized version.

items: Pattern: pattern printing where each row's length is known in advance, so it can be built directly instead of grown character by character, further batched into a single output call.

Core Idea: row i always needs exactly i stars, a length known before that row is built, so a direct repeat operation constructs it in one step, and joining every row together allows the entire pattern to be produced with a single output call.
Time: O(n squared) output calls for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized version, O(1) for the further optimized version; total characters printed are always O(n squared).
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n) for the current row being built, O(n squared) to hold the entire joined pattern in the further optimized version.
Most Important Observation: whenever a piece of output's exact size is known ahead of time, it should be constructed directly rather than grown incrementally.
Interview Difficulty: easy to produce the correct shape; recognizing that row lengths are already known, and batching output calls accordingly, is what shows real efficiency awareness.
One line memory trick: build each row directly at its known length, then batch every row into a single output call.
